questions.stem: Which statement describes species diversity?
options: The number of different species in an area and their relative abundance
The variety of alleles within the gene pool of a single species in an area
The variety of habitats, communities and ecosystems found within a region
The total number of individual organisms of all kinds living in an area
questions.explanation: Species diversity combines how many species are present (richness) with their relative abundance (evenness). The variety of alleles within one species is genetic diversity, and the variety of habitats and communities is ecosystem diversity.

questions.stem: A report finds that an isolated koala population has only one or two alleles at many gene loci where other koala populations have several. Which level of biodiversity is low in this population?
options: Species evenness
Genetic diversity
Species diversity
Ecosystem diversity
questions.explanation: Genetic diversity is the variety of alleles and genes within a population or species. The report is about one species only, so species diversity and evenness, which compare different species, do not apply.

questions.stem: A region of north Queensland contains rainforest, mangroves, open woodland, heath and fringing coral reefs. This region has high:
options: population density
ecosystem diversity
genetic diversity
species evenness
questions.explanation: Ecosystem diversity is the variety of ecosystems, habitats and communities within a region. A list of different ecosystem types says nothing directly about alleles within a species or the relative abundance of species.

questions.stem: According to the biological species concept, a species is a group of organisms that:
options: share the same physical features and overall body form
occupy the same ecological niche in one ecosystem
share at least ninety per cent of their DNA sequence
can interbreed in nature to produce fertile offspring
questions.explanation: The biological species concept defines a species by reproductive compatibility: members interbreed naturally and produce fertile offspring, and are reproductively isolated from other groups. Defining species by shared physical features is the morphological species concept, and by niche is the ecological species concept.

questions.stem: Why is the biological species concept of little use for classifying bacteria?
options: They are too small for their mating to be observed
They reproduce asexually, so interbreeding cannot be the test
They never exchange any genetic material with one another
Their DNA cannot be sequenced and compared reliably
questions.explanation: Bacteria reproduce by binary fission, an asexual process, so the test of producing fertile offspring by interbreeding does not apply. Bacteria do exchange genetic material, for example by conjugation, and bacterial DNA is routinely sequenced, which is why other species concepts are used for them.

questions.stem: A palaeontologist describes two new species of extinct kangaroo from fossil skulls. Why must she use a species concept other than the biological species concept?
options: Extinct species are not given names in the Linnaean system of classification
Kangaroos reproduce asexually, so interbreeding does not occur in the group
Whether extinct organisms could interbreed cannot be observed or tested
Fossil skulls always contain too little bone to show any physical features
questions.explanation: The biological species concept depends on whether organisms interbreed to produce fertile offspring, which cannot be tested for fossils. Palaeontologists rely mainly on physical features, the morphological species concept. Extinct species are named in the Linnaean system, and kangaroos reproduce sexually.

questions.stem: Which lists the major Linnaean taxa from the most inclusive to the least inclusive?
options: Kingdom, class, phylum, order, family, genus, species
Kingdom, phylum, order, class, family, genus, species
Kingdom, phylum, class, family, order, genus, species
Kingdom, phylum, class, order, family, genus, species
questions.explanation: The hierarchy runs kingdom, phylum, class, order, family, genus, species, with each taxon nested within the one above. A common slip is to swap class and order, or order and family.

questions.stem: In the scientific name Phascolarctos cinereus (koala), what does cinereus identify?
options: The scientist who first named the koala
The species within the genus Phascolarctos
The genus the koala belongs to
The family the koala belongs to
questions.explanation: In binomial nomenclature the genus name comes first with a capital letter and the specific name follows in lower case. The whole name is italicised in print, or underlined when handwritten.

questions.stem: Linnaeus grouped organisms mainly by their physical features. Why have many species since been moved to different groups?
options: International rules require every scientific name to be replaced each century
Species change their body shape too quickly to stay in the same group for long
Physical features cannot be measured accurately enough to be used at all
DNA evidence has shown that some similar-looking species are not closely related
questions.explanation: Physical similarity can arise without close relationship, so a system based on appearance does not always reflect evolutionary relatedness. As molecular data have become available, species have been reclassified to match their shared ancestry.

questions.stem: A key reads: 1a six legs, go to 2; 1b eight legs, spider. 2a wings present, go to 3; 2b no wings, silverfish. 3a two pairs of scaly wings, butterfly; 3b one pair of wings, fly. A specimen has six legs and one pair of wings. What is it?
options: Fly
Butterfly
Silverfish
Spider
questions.explanation: Six legs leads from step 1 to step 2, having wings leads to step 3, and one pair of wings gives fly. A butterfly has two pairs of wings, and a silverfish has no wings.

questions.stem: Why should each couplet in a dichotomous key use a feature such as 'leaves divided into leaflets' rather than 'leaves large'?
options: Each choice must be clear-cut so different users reach the same answer
Keys must use leaf features because they are the same in every plant
Size features take longer to observe than other features in the field
Each step must use a feature that only one species in the whole key shows
questions.explanation: A key works only if every choice has one clear, objective answer. 'Large' is a matter of opinion, so two people could go different ways with the same specimen. A couplet only needs to divide the remaining organisms into two groups, not single out one species.

questions.stem: Ecologists catch, mark and release 60 bush rats. A week later they catch 80, of which 12 are marked. Using the Lincoln index, N = (M × n)/m, what is the estimated population?
questions.explanation: N = (60 × 80)/12 = 4800/12 = 400. The value 4800 forgets to divide by the number of marked animals recaptured, and 16 comes from putting the recaptured marked count in the numerator.

questions.stem: Which is an assumption of the Lincoln index?
options: Marked animals mix randomly with the population before recapture
The population grows steadily between the capture and recapture
Marked animals learn to avoid traps on the second sampling occasion
Only animals of one sex are marked and then released each time
questions.explanation: The method assumes marked animals spread evenly through the population, so the marked share of the second sample matches the marked share of the whole population. It also assumes no births, deaths or migration between samples and that marking does not change behaviour or survival.

questions.stem: In a capture-recapture study of skinks, the bright paint used for marking makes marked skinks easier for birds to see and eat. How will this affect the population estimate?
options: It will overestimate the population, because fewer marked skinks are recaptured
It will underestimate the population, because fewer marked skinks are recaptured
It will overestimate the population, because more marked skinks are recaptured
It will underestimate the population, because marked skinks are easier to catch
questions.explanation: If marked skinks are eaten, the number of marked animals in the second sample (m) falls. Because m is the denominator of N = (M × n)/m, a smaller m gives a larger estimate, so the population is overestimated.

questions.stem: Sites P and Q each contain 100 birds of 4 species. At site P the counts are 25, 25, 25 and 25. At site Q they are 85, 5, 5 and 5. Which statement is correct?
options: Site Q has greater richness and greater evenness than site P
Both sites have the same richness, but site P has greater evenness
Site P has greater richness, but both sites have the same evenness
Both sites have the same evenness, but site Q has greater richness
questions.explanation: Both sites have four species, so their richness is equal. Evenness describes how equally individuals are spread among species: at site P every species is equally common, while site Q is dominated by one species.

questions.stem: A quadrat survey finds three species with 6, 3 and 1 individuals. Using SDI = 1 − (Σn(n − 1))/(N(N − 1)), what is Simpson's diversity index?
questions.explanation: N = 10, so N(N − 1) = 90. Σn(n − 1) = (6 × 5) + (3 × 2) + (1 × 0) = 36, and 36/90 = 0.40. SDI = 1 − 0.40 = 0.60. The value 0.40 forgets to subtract from 1, and 0.54 uses n² and N² instead of n(n − 1) and N(N − 1).

questions.stem: Site X has a Simpson's diversity index of 0.82 and site Y has an index of 0.35. Which conclusion is correct?
options: Site Y is more diverse: two individuals picked at random are more likely to differ in species
Site X is more diverse: it must contain more than twice as many species as site Y
Site Y is more diverse: a lower index shows that its species are more evenly spread
Site X is more diverse: two individuals picked at random are more likely to differ in species
questions.explanation: Simpson's diversity index runs from 0 to 1, and higher values mean greater diversity. It gives the probability that two individuals chosen at random belong to different species. A higher index does not tell you the number of species, because it reflects both richness and evenness.

questions.stem: A sedge is recorded in 9 of 15 quadrats along a creek. What is its percentage frequency?
questions.explanation: Percentage frequency is the number of quadrats containing the species divided by the total number of quadrats, × 100: 9/15 × 100 = 60%. The value 40% is the share of quadrats where the sedge was absent.

questions.stem: In a quadrat survey, what does percentage cover measure?
options: The number of different species recorded within each quadrat
The proportion of the quadrat area covered by a species, seen from above
The number of individuals of a species counted inside each quadrat
The proportion of all quadrats in which a species is recorded at all
questions.explanation: Percentage cover estimates how much of the quadrat's area a species occupies when viewed from above. It is useful for plants such as grasses where individuals are hard to count. The share of quadrats containing a species is percentage frequency.

questions.stem: A paddock slopes from a dry ridge down to a wet creek, and the plants change gradually down the slope. Which technique best shows how species change along this gradient?
options: Random quadrats placed anywhere across the paddock
Capture-recapture of plants growing on the ridge
A single large quadrat in the centre of the paddock
A belt transect running from the ridge to the creek
questions.explanation: A transect laid along an environmental gradient records how species composition changes with distance, and a belt transect also gives abundance data in each section. Randomly placed quadrats sample the area but do not show the pattern along the slope, and capture-recapture is for mobile animals.

questions.stem: A reserve is 70% woodland and 30% grassland. Which sampling design is stratified?
options: Place quadrats wherever the greatest number of species can be seen
Split it by habitat and place 70% of quadrats randomly in woodland, 30% in grassland
Place quadrats every 10 m along one straight line across the whole reserve
Use random-number coordinates to place quadrats anywhere in the reserve
questions.explanation: Stratified sampling divides an area into distinct strata, such as habitats, and samples each in proportion to its size. Quadrats at fixed intervals are systematic sampling, and random coordinates over the whole reserve are random sampling. Choosing species-rich spots introduces bias.

questions.stem: Students placing quadrats in a heath tend to drop them on patches with interesting flowers. Which change best reduces this bias?
options: Use a random-number generator to set each quadrat's coordinates
Use smaller quadrats so that they are easier to place accurately
Have the most experienced student choose every quadrat position
Sample only the patches with the most species to save time
questions.explanation: Random-number generators remove human choice from where samples go, so every part of the area has an equal chance of being sampled. Smaller quadrats or a single chooser do not remove the bias, and sampling only species-rich patches makes it worse.

questions.stem: Two groups count plants in quadrats at the same site. One counts only plants rooted inside the frame; the other also counts plants overhanging it. Their densities differ. What does this show?
options: The site's plants are clumped, so the two groups' results cannot agree
Quadrats cannot be used to estimate the density of plant species
The group with the higher count must have used a larger quadrat
Counting criteria must be agreed in advance so results are comparable
questions.explanation: Clear counting criteria, such as counting only plants rooted inside the frame, make sampling consistent between people and over time. Without them the difference comes from method, not from the vegetation.

questions.stem: Which is a biotic factor affecting a population of rock-wallabies?
options: Annual rainfall
Rocky shelter
Soil nutrients
Predation by foxes
questions.explanation: Biotic factors come from living things, such as predation, competition, disease and food availability. Rainfall, shelter among rocks and soil nutrients are abiotic factors.

questions.stem: Mature saltbush plants on an arid plain are spaced almost evenly, because each plant's roots draw water from the soil around it. What distribution pattern does this show?
options: Random
Stratified
Uniform
Clumped
questions.explanation: Competition for a scarce resource such as water often spaces individuals evenly, giving a uniform distribution. Clumped distributions occur where resources are patchy or offspring stay near parents, and random distributions where neither applies.

questions.stem: A fern grows only in a few moist gullies scattered through a large forest. Why might ten randomly placed quadrats give an unreliable estimate of its abundance?
options: Ferns grow too slowly for their abundance to be measured with any quadrat
Its clumped distribution means the quadrats may miss or over-sample the gullies
Its uniform distribution means every quadrat will give exactly the same result
Random quadrats can only be used where a species is spread evenly across the area
questions.explanation: When a species is confined to microhabitats, a few random quadrats may all miss the patches, or by chance land in several, giving very different estimates each time. Stratified sampling of the gullies and the surrounding forest, or more samples, would give more reliable results.

questions.stem: Along a 50 m transect away from a creek, soil moisture falls from 40% to 8%. Sedge cover falls from 80% to 0%, while spinifex cover rises from 0% to 60%. Which conclusion is best supported?
options: Sedge cover is positively correlated with soil moisture along this transect
Low soil moisture causes spinifex to outcompete the sedges along the transect
Spinifex cover is positively correlated with soil moisture along the transect
Spinifex grows faster than sedges in all soils, whatever their moisture
questions.explanation: Sedge cover is highest where soil is wettest and falls as moisture falls, a positive correlation. The data show association only, so they cannot show that dryness causes competition between the species. Spinifex cover rises as moisture falls, a negative correlation.

questions.stem: Which features of the tallest stratum does Specht's classification of Australian vegetation use?
options: Its mean annual biotemperature and annual rainfall
Its soil type, soil depth and annual rainfall
Its life form and height, and its foliage projective cover
Its species richness and Simpson's diversity index
questions.explanation: Specht's scheme names vegetation by the growth form and height of the tallest stratum (for example trees 10 to 30 m) and the foliage projective cover of that stratum. Biotemperature and precipitation are used by the Holdridge life zone scheme.

questions.stem: Using Specht's classification, a community's tallest stratum is trees about 20 m tall with a foliage projective cover of 50%. How is it classified?
options: Open forest
Woodland
Closed forest
Tall open forest
questions.explanation: For trees 10 to 30 m tall, foliage projective cover of 30 to 70% is open forest. Cover of 70 to 100% would be closed forest and 10 to 30% woodland. The 'tall' classes are for trees over 30 m.

questions.stem: A survey records that the tallest stratum is trees about 35 m tall with a foliage projective cover of 15%. Using Specht's classification, how is this community classified?
options: Tall open forest
Woodland
Tall open woodland
Tall woodland
questions.explanation: Trees over 30 m take the 'tall' classes, and cover of 10 to 30% is woodland, giving tall woodland. Tall open forest needs 30 to 70% cover, tall open woodland less than 10%, and plain woodland is for trees 10 to 30 m.

questions.stem: Which data does the Holdridge life zone classification scheme use to classify ecosystems?
options: Height and foliage projective cover of the tallest plant stratum
Species richness, species evenness and percentage cover
Soil depth, soil pH and rate of leaf litter decomposition
Biotemperature, annual precipitation and potential evapotranspiration ratio
questions.explanation: Holdridge life zones are defined by climate: mean annual biotemperature, annual precipitation and the ratio of potential evapotranspiration to precipitation, plotted on logarithmic axes. Height and foliage cover of the tallest stratum are used in Specht's classification.

questions.stem: In the Holdridge scheme, how is biotemperature different from ordinary mean annual temperature?
options: Temperatures are measured inside plant tissues rather than in the air
It is the difference between the year's highest and lowest air temperatures
Temperatures below freezing are counted as zero, as plants are then dormant
Only the temperatures recorded during the hottest month are included
questions.explanation: Biotemperature averages temperatures with values below 0 °C set to 0 °C, because plant growth effectively stops below freezing. It therefore reflects the heat available for growth rather than the average air temperature.

questions.stem: On a Holdridge life zone chart, a lowland site with a high biotemperature, very high annual precipitation and a low potential evapotranspiration ratio is classified as:
options: tropical desert
boreal moist forest
polar tundra
tropical rain forest
questions.explanation: High biotemperature places the site in the tropical region, and very high rainfall with a low potential evapotranspiration ratio means a wet (superhumid) climate, giving rain forest. A tropical desert has high biotemperature but low precipitation, and boreal and polar zones have low biotemperatures.

questions.stem: Rabbits released into a new area with abundant food and few predators increase faster and faster in number. Which growth pattern is this?
options: Logistic growth, shown as a J-shaped curve
Exponential growth, shown as a J-shaped curve
Logistic growth, shown as an S-shaped curve
Exponential growth, shown as an S-shaped curve
questions.explanation: When resources are not limiting, a population grows by a constant proportion each generation, so numbers rise ever faster: exponential growth, which plots as a J-curve. Logistic growth gives an S-curve that levels off at the carrying capacity.

questions.stem: In logistic growth, why does the rate of population growth slow as the population nears the carrying capacity?
options: Death rates fall to zero once the population stops increasing
Limiting factors such as food and space become scarcer as density rises
Individuals stop reproducing once the population reaches a set size
Immigration always increases as a population becomes more crowded
questions.explanation: As the population grows, competition for limited resources increases, so the birth rate falls and the death rate rises. Growth slows and the population levels off where births and deaths balance, at the carrying capacity.

questions.stem: Which set of features is typical of an r-strategist?
options: Many small offspring, early maturity, little parental care
Few large offspring, late maturity, much parental care
Many small offspring, late maturity, much parental care
Few large offspring, early maturity, little parental care
questions.explanation: r-strategists invest little in each of many offspring and reproduce early, so they can increase rapidly when conditions allow. K-strategists have few offspring, mature late, care for their young and tend to have populations near the carrying capacity.

questions.stem: An ecologist finds that a species' population rises rapidly after rain, then crashes within weeks, and rarely levels off. Which strategy and growth curve does this species most likely show?
options: An r-strategy, with S-shaped growth held close to the carrying capacity
A K-strategy, with J-shaped bursts of growth and sudden crashes
An r-strategy, with J-shaped bursts of growth and sudden crashes
A K-strategy, with S-shaped growth that levels off at the carrying capacity
questions.explanation: Rapid booms followed by crashes in unpredictable environments are typical of r-strategists, whose populations grow almost exponentially while conditions last. K-strategists tend to follow logistic growth and stay near the carrying capacity.

questions.stem: A population of 500 lizards has 80 births, 30 deaths, 10 immigrants and 20 emigrants in a year. What is the population change and growth rate for the year?
options: An increase of 50, a growth rate of 10%
An increase of 80, a growth rate of 16%
An increase of 60, a growth rate of 12%
An increase of 40, a growth rate of 8%
questions.explanation: Change = (births + immigrants) − (deaths + emigrants) = (80 + 10) − (30 + 20) = 40, and 40/500 × 100 = 8%. An increase of 50 ignores migration, and 80 wrongly adds the emigrants as a gain.

questions.stem: A population of 1200 fruit bats has 150 births, 210 deaths, 30 immigrants and 90 emigrants in a year. What is the growth rate for the year?
questions.explanation: Change = (150 + 30) − (210 + 90) = 180 − 300 = −120, and −120/1200 × 100 = −10%. Ignoring migration gives −60 or −5%, and adding emigrants as a gain gives +60 or +5%.
